In Australia, there is a public health care system at the federal level. It is mandatory for every one to participate in. If you do not have health insurance, they tax you. You have a significantly reduced tax (if not completely removed if you are at a lower income) for having health insurance. The reason for this is because most of the cost of a non standard medical issue (Like seeing a doctor for a cold), is covered by the private insurer and thus saves the government money, thus allowing more of it to go to those who don't have it. For basic medical stuff its free for every one, with or without health insurance. There are private and public hospitals. Public hostipals are less of a holiday than private ones and often you will get shared rooms where as in private ones you dont. Also often the waiting time for a public hospital operation is 1000% to 2000% longer than a private one. Mainly because a lot of people do not have insurance.

The cost of having insurance vs the cost of not having insurance and being taxed is not really debatable. Even with a public hospital, if its pretty serious you still have to pay. It is just subsidised by the public system. And often you would spend as much as if you just had the insurance for a couple of years.

If you have a children and they are privately insured you also get slightly less tax.
Japan is similar but without the free and private back up plans. It's cheap so people just pay in.

The penalty fee was a gamble put in by the GOP as a requirement for support, expecting to delay the bill. The DNC in turn shrugged and accepted it. The logic presented is: It was to keep costs down for insurance companies, since they were now required to accept pre-existing conditions (read: High cost patients) the offset required would be to have more healthy people paying premiums. The fee is meant as an incentive for people to sign up for a plan-if one is paying possibly the same as having a plan as not-it makes more sense to get the plan sort of thing.
